item.title: AI tools are aiding would-be spies
item.description:
AI tools are now exacerbating a largely hidden problem that frontier AI companies have been contending with for years: the risk that employees will exploit their access to spy on their employers.

Why it matters: The same AI tools that companies are racing to release can also help people plan crimes and develop the technology to carry them out, creating another security headache for the companies building them.

Driving the news: Federal prosecutors charged Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national who has been an OpenAI engineer since July 2025, with allegedly attempting to intercept private conversations at OpenAI.

  • Around Sept. 30, the company found a "surreptitious audio recording device" that was plugged into a USB port in the back of a television in an executive conference room.
  • OpenAI said in a post on X that it used its own AI models to help "understand the device and where it had come from."

Zoom in: Investigators allege Alfozan used AI tools to research company meeting rooms and develop recording equipment, according to an FBI affidavit.

  • Alfozan used a "productivity agent" to ask basic information about OpenAI's offices, the documents say. Those queries included: "What meeting was this presented at and when was it record?," "List meeting rooms in (company) that are 6+", and "can you list today's meeting in this room."
  • Investigators also said that an AI chatbot account tied to his spouse asked the model to build a "continuous audio recorder" and to add "browser access an controls," as well as encrypt the memory card where the recordings were saved.
  • The complaint didn't say whether any sensitive conversations were successfully recorded.

The big picture: This is just the latest case where AI tools have helped people carry out alleged crimes.

  • Prosecutors say they discovered a Nebraska man's use of ChatGPT before a bank robbery, including asking the model for assistance with stripping and repairing a handgun. He was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison in August.
  • Last year, authorities said a man used ChatGPT to help plot the explosion of a Tesla Cybertruck outside of the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas.

Flashback: Alfozan's case has caught viral attention across news sites and social media, but it isn't the first time a tech employee has been arrested for allegedly stealing AI trade secrets.

  • In 2024, the Justice Department indicted ex-Google software engineer Linwei Ding for stealing AI technology secrets and sharing them with two Chinese companies.
  • Earlier this year, a federal jury found Ding guilty on several counts of economic espionage and theft of trade secrets.

Threat level: Now, AI tools are adding a new dimension to corporate espionage, potentially making it easier for less-sophisticated actors to build spying devices while giving investigators new ways to retrace their steps.

The bottom line: AI models are creating security headaches for companies not only when they break out of containment, but also when people use them to plan and carry out crimes — including espionage against their own internal workings.

item.title: New inflation warning sign
item.description:
America's inflation problem is becoming harder to contain, with new evidence Wednesday that price pressures are extending beyond the war-related energy shock rattling the global economy.

Why it matters: Inflation is squeezing household budgets and dimming hopes for relief. It is also increasing the prospect that the Fed will have to raise interest rates further.

What they're saying: "Higher energy costs are beginning to seep into broader services prices, increasing the risk that this inflation burst will persist," Fitch Ratings economist Olu Sonola wrote in a note.

  • The Consumer Price Index report "stands out as the first of the year in which price pressure appeared to be showing up in most corners of the consumption basket at once," Glenmede's Jason Pride wrote.

By the numbers: The CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, accelerating from August's 0.4% increase. The index increased 3.7% in the 12 months through September, compared with 3.4% in the prior month.

  • Gasoline prices surged 9% in September, accounting for more than half of the monthly jump in consumer prices.
  • Core prices, which exclude food and energy, advanced 0.3% for the second consecutive month. The annual rate accelerated to 2.6% from 2.4%.

The intrigue: Over the past three months, core CPI has risen at a 3.4% annualized rate, up notably from 2% in August — a sign that underlying inflation pressures are strengthening.

  • Inflation was stubborn in parts of the services economy that are less directly exposed to the energy price surge.
  • Shelter costs accelerated last month, rising 0.4%, while used car prices climbed 0.7%. Airfares jumped 1.2% as airlines grappled with soaring jet fuel costs.
  • "Supercore" — a narrower measure of inflation that excludes housing and energy services — was hot again last month. Prices in that category have risen at a nearly 4.6% annualized rate over the past three months.

The big picture: Top Fed officials in recent days have played down the urgency of another interest rate hike later this month. But Wednesday's inflation data swiftly revived bets that the central bank will have to act sooner than the following meeting, in December.

  • The two-year Treasury yield — particularly sensitive to Fed policy expectations — jumped roughly 12 basis points after the report.
  • Traders now see a 47% chance of a quarter-point rate hike at the Oct. 27–28 policy meeting, up from 22.1% yesterday (and 18% this time last week), according to CME FedWatch.

What to watch: Fed governor Christopher Waller told Bloomberg Tuesday that rising Treasury yields could help cool the economy, potentially reducing the need for another rate hike.

  • But the inflation report complicates that argument — showing that underlying price pressures remain stubbornly elevated.
  • Instead, the report lends support to more hawkish policymakers like Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, who warned Monday that inflation was "relatively broad-based rather than concentrated in one component."
  • Hammack cited tariffs, the AI investment boom and rising services prices as additional sources of price pressures.

The bottom line: For American consumers, the risk is that another bout of inflation proves harder to shake — prolonging the affordability squeeze while keeping borrowing costs elevated.

  • The squeeze is already showing up in paychecks, with inflation outpacing wage growth for six consecutive months.
  • Real average hourly earnings fell 0.5% in September and were down 0.7% from a year earlier.

item.title: Social Security recipients will see rise in monthly payments next year
item.description:
Data: Social Security Administration; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios

Social Security recipients will see the largest rise in their monthly payments in four years in January, with a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment.

Driving the news: The Social Security Administration announced the 2027 COLA adjustment for 76 million recipients of retirement and disability benefits, which by law is calculated based on the Consumer Price Index for the July-through-September quarter.

  • That will increase the average retiree's benefits by $900 a year, or $75 a month.
  • The agency also said that the cutoff for Social Security taxes will rise to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 this year. Income above that threshold is not subject to payroll tax.

How it works: The adjustment is, by statute, determined by the year-over-year change in CPI for the third quarter. Thus, the September data released this morning was the final input needed to calculate the adjustment.

Between the lines: The adjustment will mean more nominal income for seniors and disability recipients, amounting to a mild fiscal stimulus come January.

  • However, it also accelerates Social Security's looming fiscal problems, with its trust fund scheduled to expire in six years.
  • The most recent projections issued by the program's trustees assumed a 0.9 percentage point lower COLA for 2027, the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget notes.

item.title: Inflation heats up as gas prices surge
item.description:
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

U.S. inflation picked up in September as soaring energy prices added to already stubborn price pressures, the Labor Department said on Wednesday.

Why it matters: The latest Consumer Price Index shows that the inflation fight is far from over — and makes further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes more likely as Americans struggle with higher costs.

By the numbers: CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, with the annual inflation rate at 3.7%, the government said.

  • That compares with a 0.4% monthly increase and a 3.4% annual rate in August.
  • Core prices, which exclude volatile food and energy costs, gained 0.3% on the month, compared with a similar monthly gain in August. In the 12 months through September, core CPI rose 2.6%, up from 2.4% the prior month.

Zoom in: The latest figures capture the toll of the Middle East war on American consumers as disruptions to global energy supplies push up fuel prices.

  • Gasoline prices spiked 9.1% in September after climbing 3.9% in August, when they accounted for more than a third of the monthly increase in consumer prices.
  • Prices for shelter, one of the largest components of the index, increased 0.4%, compared with a 0.3% gain in August.
  • Food prices were flat, compared with a slight 0.1% increase the previous month.

Zoom out: The surge in fuel prices has prompted extraordinary measures from the Trump administration, particularly as soaring diesel costs threaten to push up prices for goods transported across the country.

  • President Trump temporarily eased restrictions on tax-exempt diesel and lifted some U.S. sanctions on Russian fuel to boost global diesel supplies.
  • Airline fares surged 1.2% in September — bringing the annual increase to 22% — as higher jet fuel costs put pressure on ticket prices.

What to watch: The Social Security Administration is set to announce the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment for millions of retirees, based on inflation figures released on Wednesday.

  • The increase will take effect in January.

The big picture: The report comes as Federal Reserve officials weigh how soon to raise interest rates again, with policymakers divided over the persistence of inflation.

  • In a speech on Monday, Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack warned that inflation pressures extend well beyond energy — citing tariffs, AI investment and rising services prices.
  • Fed governor Christopher Waller told Bloomberg on Tuesday that higher Treasury yields are already helping restrain economic activity, possibly reducing the urgency of another rate hike this month.
  • New York Fed president John Williams said one more increase might be ahead this year, though he cautioned the central bank might not have to raise again in 2027.

The bottom line: In the wake of the inflation report, financial markets are now betting that an interest rate increase is more likely when the Fed meets later this month.

  • Odds of October rate hike jumped to 44% from 22% Tuesday, according to CME FedWatch data.
  • The yield on the two-year Treasury note — the security most reactive to Fed policy expectations — jumped 12 basis points, while the 10-year Treasury yield rose 7 basis points.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

item.title: Apple bets AI can finally make us want a smart home
item.description:
Apple's big new hardware bet for the AI era is here, and it's a...smart display?

Why it matters: Cue the time machine and let's head back to 2014, when Amazon's Alexa shocked the tech world and led us to imagine a Jetsons-style home would be ours in the near future.

  • It wasn't, but Apple believes it could come soon. The iPhone maker is betting that modern AI can finally make good on that vision, unveiling a slew of new smart home devices Tuesday.

Between the lines: While the smart home has largely failed to live up to its promise, modern AI could help address its biggest shortcoming: Getting devices to just work without requiring users to become amateur IT experts.

  • Apple's new products emphasize easy setup and integration with its existing ecosystem, while AI could help diagnose problems and coordinate devices.
  • "The capabilities that AI would bring in helping make sure that these devices can solve their own problems and work together is really interesting to me," Paul Gagnon, a vice president at market research firm Circana, told Axios.

Driving the news: Apple's announcements Tuesday included a new smart display, a revamped speaker, an updated streaming device and a collection of connected home accessories developed with partners.

  • HomeView: Apple's new $299 smart display features a 7-inch screen and an AI-powered Siri that can respond to requests, control connected devices and recognize different household members to deliver personalized information. It will ship next month and comes in two versions, one that can hang on a wall and the other, a tabletop device reminiscent of the iMac G4.
  • Apple Home Collection: Apple worked with LG and Schneider Electric on smart locks, doorbells, cameras and thermostats designed to work together through Apple's Home app and Siri.

The big picture: The AI hardware race is taking two different paths: Making familiar devices substantially smarter and creating entirely new kinds of gadgets.

  • Amazon and Google have been incorporating more capabilities into their respective assistants and accompanying smart home products, efforts that were three years in the making.
  • Meanwhile, others are betting that the AI era needs new kinds of highly personal devices. OpenAI is expected to release its first AI device soon, and Meta recently teased plans for Charm, a Tamagotchi-like device meant to bring its Muse assistant to the masses.

Reality check: Apple has a loyal customer base and a history of making complicated technology easier to use. But that doesn't guarantee consumers will spend more on a category that has struggled to generate sustained demand.

  • U.S. smart speaker dollar sales fell 9% in 2024 and another 7% in 2025, and smart displays fared poorly as well before rebounding somewhat this year, according to Circana.
  • "We have definitely been in a, we'll call it, an enthusiast phase or early adopters phase for quite a while now," said Circana's Gagnon.

Zoom out: Better AI doesn't necessarily mean consumers will rush to buy more smart home devices, particularly when increasingly capable AI assistants are already available on smartphones.

  • Apple could benefit from its large installed base of iPhone owners and its ability to simplify setup, but it remains unclear whether those advantages will expand what has remained a niche market.

"The new smart home products could appeal to consumers who have previously resisted buying smart home devices because they are perceived as difficult to set up and sometimes hard to use," Ben Wood, chief analyst of CCS Insight, told Axios.

The bottom line: A decade ago, the smart home promised to change how we live. AI may finally make that possible. But Apple still has to convince consumers that the home needs another screen or speaker — not just a smarter phone.

item.title: AI's extreme heat challenge is moving from prediction to protection
item.description:
Cities and researchers are using AI to map and predict extreme heat risk, but new research suggests it's used far more to identify where people are in danger than to help officials respond.

Why it matters: As climate change intensifies extreme heat, better predictions won't protect vulnerable communities unless governments can turn them into action.

  • U.S. deaths associated with high temperatures rose 53% from an annual average of 2,670 in 2000–2009 to more than 4,000 in 2010–2020, according to a 2025 Yale study.

Driving the news: A study published in Climate Risk Management examined existing research on how AI and machine learning are being used to manage extreme heat.

  • Of the research papers reviewed, 98.4% focused on prediction and 59.2% on prevention. That's compared with just 10.4% on response, 3.2% on recovery and 1.6% on preparedness — a disparity the authors call a "research-to-implementation gap."
  • The research is heavily focused on using AI to forecast dangerous heat and identify who's at risk, with far less attention on how it can help officials decide what to do next.
  • "Where AI can actually add value is where prediction is central to the decision-making, and that's in scale or providing more granularity," said Karishma V. Patel, a RAND policy researcher who co-authored the study.

State of play: Turning sophisticated heat predictions into government action requires more than advanced models.

  • Cornell researcher Jennah Gosciak told Axios that having "robust data systems" that can ingest data from a variety of sources and then make it usable to practitioners "is most of the battle here."

Case in point: Google in June announced it had expanded its AI-powered Heat Resilience data from an initial 14-city pilot to more than 50 cities worldwide, giving urban planners building-level data to help target heat interventions.

  • The data uses AI and high-resolution imagery to map roof reflectivity down to individual buildings.
  • Google said data from the pilots helped inform decisions in several cities, including cool-roof ordinances and adaptation plans.

Reality check: Better information doesn't necessarily equal better outcomes.

  • Gosciak, who spent time as a Public Interest Technology Fellow with New York City Emergency Management, recently compared simpler heat-vulnerability indexes with more complex predictive algorithms for government heat decisions.
  • She described one important distinction as "slow versus fast data." Predictive algorithms may be more useful for time-sensitive decisions "tied to a specific trigger event," while simpler indexes can be better suited to longer-term planning.
  • One advantage of simpler indexes is that officials can explicitly choose which vulnerable populations to prioritize, added Gosciak, a PhD student in Cornell's Information Science Department.

What's next: The next frontier may be less about making heat forecasts incrementally better and more about connecting predictions to interventions.

  • AI's value could lie in helping officials make "near real-time decisions" by integrating changing signals and providing "hyperlocal forecasting at granular levels," Patel said.
  • That could help officials respond to heat risks in real time and better understand compound threats involving heat, air pollution, wildfire smoke and drought, she said.

The bottom line: "What is important is not just that we can build AI-enabled technology, but it actually solves a problem or removes a bottleneck," Patel said.

  • AI's value could lie in helping officials make "near real-time decisions" by integrating changing signals and providing "hyperlocal forecasting at granular levels," Patel said.

item.title: Bank of America hit with $1.2 billion penalty over money laundering allegations
item.description:
The Treasury Department on Tuesday announced more than $1.2 billion in penalties against Bank of America for years of failures to report suspicious transactions and address shortcomings in its anti-money-laundering program.

Why it matters: The action includes the third-largest penalty in Treasury history.

What they're saying: "Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a press release.

The big picture: The civil action comes less than a week after federal regulators fined American Express $350 million over similar failures to detect and report suspected money laundering.

Zoom in: Bank of America admitted to willfully violating federal anti-money-laundering laws — including requirements to maintain adequate safeguards and report suspicious transactions.

  • Regulators said the bank failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions, resulting in more than $5 billion in suspicious activity that was either unreported or reported late.
  • More than $1 billion involved potential national security and other high-priority risks — including Chinese money-laundering networks and suspected trade-based money laundering linked to the U.S.-Mexico border, regulators said.

Of note: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency also assessed a $750 million civil penalty, the largest in the agency's history.

  • Treasury also announced an $11.6 million settlement with Bank of America over hundreds of apparent violations of U.S. sanctions, including those targeting Russia and Iran.

Flashback: Bank of America has been working to address deficiencies in its anti-money-laundering program since a December 2024 regulatory order. But regulators said significant problems persisted.

  • Officials said the bank prioritized revenue while limiting compliance resources — at times relying on law enforcement and other outside sources to identify suspicious activity.

The other side: In a statement, Bank of America said it has invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to fighting financial crime.

  • "Our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators."

What to watch: Bank of America reports third-quarter earnings Wednesday. The bank said it will record a $1.2 billion, non-tax-deductible charge in those results.

  • The bank said costs associated with its ongoing efforts to fix compliance problems are already reflected in its expenses.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

item.title: Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer
item.description:
Pope Leo has been diagnosed with lung cancer, the Vatican said Tuesday.

Why it matters: The Vatican disclosed the pontiff's health news just hours after he underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung.

What they're saying: "The surgery was completed successfully, within the expected timeframe and as planned, and the holy father has returned to his room," per a Holy See Press Office statement published Tuesday.

  • The office said in that statement it would provide more information shortly, and later followed up with news of Leo's diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, which they said tests "conducted beforehand" had led them to suspect.

Driving the news: The first American pontiff was admitted to Rome's Agostino Gemelli University Hospital on Tuesday afternoon for surgery.

  • "The Pope was in the operating room approximately three hours, while the operation itself lasted about 90 minutes. The doctors said it was successful and there were no complications," the statement said.
  • The Catholic Church leader carried out his usual duties Monday and was greeted by supporters and patients at the hospital, according to the Vatican statement.

Zoom in: Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer, per the Cancer Center.

  • It forms when the cells lining the outside of the lungs become cancerous. Its symptoms include persistent cough, shortness of breath and chest pain, amongst other things.
  • Patients with adenocarcinoma don't always experience symptoms early on, and it is often detected during a scan for a medical reason unrelated to lung cancer.

The big picture: Doctors discovered the nodule during routine medical checkups.

  • Leo said Sunday that the nodule "was detected at a very early stage and is well localized."
  • He thanked his supporters for their "spiritual closeness" and said he was entrusting himself to their prayers.

Go deeper: Pope Leo to have "nodule" removed from lung

item.title: Companies are building with AI — and exposing new security risks
item.description:
The amount of AI-related infrastructure exposed to the public internet jumped 63% in nine months, according to new Censys data shared first with Axios.

Why it matters: The AI boom isn't just creating new models and chatbots. It's creating a sprawling layer of software that companies will also need to inventory, patch and secure.

Threat level: Many of these tools connect AI applications to sensitive corporate data and other services, creating potential entry points for hackers looking to access company systems.

  • "It's a little bit beyond just like the tool itself, but these [tools] talk to some really sensitive systems," Emily Austin, a principal researcher at Censys and co-author of the report, told Axios.

The big picture: Censys identified nearly 268,000 internet-facing systems running 44 different AI-related products as of July, up from roughly 164,000 in October 2025.

  • These include the software used to connect AI models to databases, corporate applications and other services.

Between the lines: The ease of building and hosting AI applications is making it harder for companies to keep track of what software employees are using and whether it's secure.

  • Censys CEO Zakir Durumeric told Axios that companies were already struggling to keep track of their existing software even before employees started building their own AI applications.
  • These new AI apps can often connect to sensitive company information, such as emails, financial records and internal databases.

Zoom in: The most widely exposed product was n8n, a workflow automation platform that can connect AI agents to other applications and services.

  • Censys found nearly 114,000 internet-facing deployments of n8n, including roughly 77,000 running software versions affected by at least one recently disclosed critical vulnerability.
  • Researchers also found more than 54,000 exposed control panels for OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent that users can connect to personal accounts and other services.

Yes, but: The findings don't establish whether those deployments are actually vulnerable to exploitation, but they highlight the risks of exposing software that can access sensitive company systems.

The bottom line: Companies need to treat AI infrastructure like any other software they deploy, Austin said, including regularly reviewing, updating and securing the systems.

item.title: A golden age of corporate profits
item.description:
Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips; Note: After-tax profit data includes inventory and capital depreciation adjustments.

Corporate America is raking in record profits, luxuriating in luscious margins and capturing the largest chunk of the country's income on record.

Why it matters: The corporate bonanza is bolstering the stock market, but it may also be playing a role in the persistently sour sentiment among the American electorate.

The latest: Tuesday is the unofficial start of third-quarter earnings season as JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs and others report results.

Zoom in: Wall Street expects the members of the blue-chip S&P 500 index to continue to make it rain.

  • Third-quarter earnings per share are expected to grow roughly 29% for the index, compared with the quarter in 2025, according to estimate data collected by FactSet.
  • That's after a massive 50% annual increase in second-quarter earnings that was supercharged by the giant, non-operating gains on valuations of tech investments reported by Amazon and Alphabet. (Amazon, for example, penciled in its stake in Anthropic as boosting its profit by more than $50 billion.)
  • But even without those enormous gains, the numbers were quite strong, thanks to the AI boom that analysts expect to keep powering giant profits.

What they're saying: The market is still all about AI, but the gains are extremely concentrated.

  • "At the stock level, AI infrastructure stocks are expected to drive more than half of S&P 500 EPS growth in Q3," wrote Ben Snider, chief U.S. equity analyst with Goldman Sachs.
  • Snider noted that more than two-thirds of the total growth in S&P 500 earnings for the quarter is expected to come from just 10 stocks.
  • What's more, Micron Technology and Nvidia alone are expected to generate more than one-third of the growth in earnings for the blue chips, Snider wrote.

The big picture: Broader measures of U.S. corporate profitability captured by economic — rather than stock market — data also seem to show remarkable strength.

  • For the economy as a whole, after-tax corporate profits in Q2 jumped 18.2% compared with the same quarter of 2025.
  • And key measures of corporate profit margins across the entire U.S. economy are some of the fattest on record.
Data: FactSet, U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips; Note: After-tax U.S. corporate profits, including inventory and capital consumption adjustments as a share of gross value added of U.S. corporate business. Reflects profits made within the U.S.; does not include profits produced overseas.

The other side: Boom times for corporate America have a flip side, however, with the so-called labor share of national income collapsing to some of the lowest levels on record.

  • The labor share tells you what percentage of the giant paycheck produced by the U.S. economy goes to workers in the form of wages and benefits, rather than to corporate profits, dividends, rents and interest paid to other economic actors, commonly summarized as "capital."

The bottom line: That decline helps explain the persistently sour mood of the American public toward the economy and its deep skepticism toward the AI boom that's producing this bonanza for American corporations.

item.title: Every major Nvidia customer is now a competitor as Microsoft reveals new Maia chip
item.description:
The trillion-dollar AI race is moving from software to silicon, as Microsoft's massive bet on its proprietary Maia chips proves Big Tech wants to wean itself off Nvidia's dominance.

Why it matters: Microsoft's plan to power its AI products with custom silicon shows how every major Nvidia customer is now a competitor, seeking lower costs, improved performance and more control.

  • The shift is particularly significant for inference — the computing needed to generate AI responses — as more sophisticated AI models and agents drive demand for computing power.

Driving the news: Microsoft unveiled Maia 300, its latest custom AI accelerator, saying it will begin deploying the chip in 2027 and it will become the primary inference system for its own products and services.

  • The company says Maia 300 will deliver 40% more AI tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems.
  • It's also designed to minimize unnecessary data movement between chips and memory, a growing bottleneck as AI models become more complex.

The big picture: Microsoft's plan is part of a much broader shift, with nearly all major AI players seeking Nvidia alternatives.

  • Google has been developing its own Tensor Processing Units for years, with its latest generation including separate versions optimized for training AI models and running inference.
  • OpenAI is developing its Jalapeño chip with Broadcom, initially focusing on inference workloads. The company said in August that its first chip was outperforming Nvidia hardware on certain workloads and that it was already developing subsequent generations.
  • Amazon has its own ⁠Trainium family of AI chips, which are being used by customers including Anthropic. OpenAI has also committed to using Amazon's custom silicon as part of a massive infrastructure agreement.
  • Anthropic confirmed in August that it is exploring its own chip designs, even as it continues to rely on chips from Nvidia, Amazon and other suppliers.
  • Meta also has an internal chip development program, while continuing to buy substantial computing capacity from Nvidia and other suppliers.

Between the lines: Nvidia isn't necessarily losing business just because its customers are developing competing chips.

  • Nvidia's revenue more than doubled to $96 billion in the second quarter, a reminder that overall demand for AI computing leaves room for Nvidia chips and new offerings from Microsoft and others.
  • Like Microsoft, most Nvidia competitors are focused on inference, where margins are highest, while Nvidia remains dominant for training.
  • Still, Nvidia has begun to leverage its balance sheet to bankroll the AI buildout, so any competition that even slightly reduces its strength is noteworthy because it could weaken its centrality to continued growth.

What they're saying: Building competitive AI hardware requires designing entire systems, optimizing everything from memory and networking to software and power consumption, Rani Borkar, Microsoft's president of Azure Hardware Systems and Infrastructure, told Axios.

  • "We prioritize Maia for inference," Borkar said, describing it as the largest and fastest-growing opportunity for AI computing and an area where Microsoft can distinguish itself on cost and efficiency.
  • "For us, it's not an either-or strategy," she said. "We want a broad ecosystem while investing deeply in our first-party silicon."

Yes, but: Microsoft's plans to make Maia its primary inference platform apply specifically to Microsoft's own services, not necessarily to third-party Azure customers, including OpenAI.

  • Borkar also cautioned that the shift won't happen overnight. Maia 300 deployments will begin in 2027, but reaching multi-gigawatt scale will take time, extending beyond next year.

Reality check: As Axios ⁠previously reported, companies developing their own chips remain dependent on the same limited manufacturing capacity, advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory that Nvidia relies on.

  • That means even if custom chips can reduce dependence on Nvidia, they don't eliminate broader supply-chain constraints.

The bottom line: Nvidia remains central to the AI boom, but its biggest customers increasingly want to control more of the technology powering their own services — and capture more of the economic benefits for themselves.

item.title: Two U.S. professors win Nobel prize in economics
item.description:
Stanford University's Robert E. Hall and Columbia University's Michael Woodford won the Nobel Prize in economics for research on how policymakers can stabilize economies, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said on Monday.

Why it matters: Their work helped shape how central banks set interest rates and communicate policy. The win comes as those institutions fight energy-driven inflation and risks to economic growth.

Zoom out: For decades, policymakers relied on economic models that linked higher inflation with lower unemployment. But that framework broke down during the 1970s stagflation when both prices and joblessness surged at the same time.

  • "The solution by Robert Hall and Michael Woodford was to build a new framework ground up," Timo Boppart, a member of the Nobel economics prize committee, said on Monday.

What they're saying: Woodford, who called into Monday's press conference hosted by the committee, said he was "elated" by the win.

  • "It's a tremendous honor. It's a surprise — but I'm feeling very good about it," Woodford said.

The intrigue: Asked by a reporter about the threat to the global economy, Woodford said the Middle East conflict has disrupted energy markets and driven price changes with consequences far beyond the region.

  • He pointed to the 2008 financial crisis as a key test of his research, when central banks cut interest rates to near zero but struggled to revive economic activity.
  • His framework helped explain how other tools, including forward guidance and asset purchases, could support the economy.

Zoom in: In research culminating in a landmark 2003 book, Woodford developed a framework linking businesses' pricing decisions to inflation and monetary policy.

  • Hall — a Stanford professor who chaired the committee that dates U.S. recessions for 46 years — showed in a 1978 paper how consumers' spending decisions reflect expectations about future income.

Of note: The prize comes with an award of 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), up from 11 million kronor last year, to be divided between the two winners.

Flashback: Recent economics Nobels have recognized research on technological progress, economic prosperity and labor markets.

  • Last year's prize went to Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt for their work explaining how innovation drives economic growth.
  • In 2024, Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson won for their research on how institutions shape economic prosperity.
  • Harvard economist Claudia Goldin won in 2023 for research that advanced the world's understanding of women's labor market outcomes.

item.title: Silicon Valley's horror shows
item.description:
Hollywood's hottest villain right now is the tech billionaire.

  • Four films hitting theaters this fall put some of Silicon Valley's most powerful and controversial figures in the spotlight: Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman and Elizabeth Holmes.

Why it matters: Hollywood's portrayal of Silicon Valley and its leaders is getting darker as negative headlines about the tech industry seep into pop culture.

  • Once portrayed as brilliant but flawed innovators, tech leaders are increasingly being cast as creepy villains whose ambitions may do more harm than good.

Zoom in: This fall's tech billionaire films span genres, from documentaries to thrillers.

  • 💻 "The Social Reckoning," Aaron Sorkin's follow-up to his 2010 hit, "The Social Network," opened Friday with Jeremy Strong portraying a more sinister Mark Zuckerberg during the 2021 Facebook whistleblower leak. Sorkin takes some cinematic liberties with chronology and other details.
  • 🚀 "Musk," the four-hour documentary (including a 10-minute intermission) about Elon Musk's rise, is playing in select theaters and opens nationwide on Friday. The roller-coaster rollout of the film, directed by Oscar-winning documentarian Alex Gibney, included critical acclaim at the Venice Film Festival and legal threats from Musk's team.
  • 🩸 "You Can See Everything," out Friday, is an experimental documentary from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim that follows ex-Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks before she went to prison. The studio, A24, says an "intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss." (More on the film.)
  • 🤖 "Artificial," a drama directed by Luca Guadagnino, stars Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and hits theaters Christmas Day. In the film, "[Garfield] depicts Altman as a manipulative, power-hungry psychopath who lies as easily as he breathes and will use anyone, anytime, anywhere to get what he wants," The Verge reports. The studio, NEON, calls it "the story of OpenAI and a two-decade artificial intelligence arms race. ... As the technology becomes more powerful and more valuable than anyone ever imagined, a battle rages over who should control the tech that could change the fate of humanity."

These projects represent a sharp turn away from some earlier movies and documentaries about Silicon Valley, like "Jobs" and "Something Ventured," which celebrated the ingenuity of founders and venture capitalists.

  • "With tech, it was an ardent love affair," says Margaret O'Mara, a University of Washington historian who studies Silicon Valley. "And when you fall out of love, you fall out of love fast."
  • "Our popular understanding of Silicon Valley and the products it makes has changed drastically."

Zoom out: Hollywood is reflecting the public's growing disillusionment with the tech industry.

  • Polls show Americans of all ages are quickly souring on AI and think it's moving too fast. Two in three Americans say social media has been bad for democracy, per Pew Research Center polling.
  • "Popular movies hold up a mirror to current social anxieties," says writer and editor-in-chief of Film Quarterly J.M. Tyree. Right now, "people are thinking about power consolidating in the hands of the few at the expense of the many."

The intrigue: Tech founders are compelling on-screen villains, Tyree says.

  • They bring together two archetypes: the ruthless businessman who's corrupted by greed, as seen in movies like "Citizen Kane" and "The Wolf of Wall Street," and the mad scientist who's morally ambiguous and employs science and technology recklessly, like in "Metropolis" or "Frankenstein."
  • Plus, their eccentricities make for good entertainment.

The bottom line: O'Mara, the Silicon Valley historian, notes: "One thing I have learned from studying the history of rich people is that extreme wealth makes you weird."

item.title: Pope Leo to have "nodule" removed from lung
item.description:
Pope Leo said Sunday tests had discovered a nodule in his lung, which he will have removed surgically this week.

The big picture: The first American pontiff, aged 71, is less than 18 months into a papacy that has been defined by public stances at odds with the White House, including clashes over immigration and deep skepticism about AI.

What he's saying: "Dear friends, during some recent medical examinations, doctors found a localized nodule in my lung. It was detected at a very early stage and is well localized. The doctors believe surgery is appropriate," the pope said during public remarks, per a translation from the Vatican.

  • "Following their advice, I have therefore decided to undergo an operation to remove it. The operation is already scheduled for the coming days. I thank you for your spiritual closeness and entrust myself to your prayers."

The pope did not explicitly say the nodule was malignant.

  • Vatican officials later said the operation would be in the next few days and the recovery would take about a week.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

item.title: As youth sports booms, churches compete for American families' Sundays
item.description:
America's youth sports boom is quietly rewriting Sunday mornings, turning the family calendar into a competition between the pews and the playing fields.

Why it matters: For generations, churches helped organize American family life around a shared weekly ritual. Youth sports are increasingly filling that role on Sundays — reshaping what families treat as sacred time.

  • The U.S. has undergone one of its fastest religious shifts in modern history, marked by a rapid increase in the religiously unaffiliated and in church closures. Youth sports are one of the less visible forces driving that broader cultural change.
  • As it's boomed into a multi-billion-dollar industry, more games are moving to Sundays, something less common a generation ago.
  • "The idea of missing church for sports is just assumed," Linda Flanagan, author of "Take Back the Game: How Money and Mania Are Ruining Kids' Sports — and Why It Matters," tells Axios. "It's just not even a consideration anymore."

By the numbers: Among parents of children ages 5-17, Sunday religious participation fell from 26.8% in 2003-07 to 16.7% in 2021-24, an Axios analysis of American Time Use Survey data found.

  • Meanwhile, youth sports participation climbed to 58% in 2024, up from 53.8% in 2022 and marking a third consecutive annual increase, according to the Aspen Institute's Project Play.
  • Another measure found 65% tried a sport at least once — the highest share in Sports & Fitness Industry Association data dating to at least 2012, the Aspen Institute's Project Play found.

State of play: The youth-sports industrial complex is rapidly commercializing, fueled by private equity, massive tournament complexes and the normalization of out-of-state travel teams.

  • Parents are increasingly treating sports not just as recreation, but as a primary identity and community anchor.

How it works: Youth sports often start in local rec leagues, then move into club and travel teams that play weekend tournaments across a wider region.

  • Across basketball, baseball, softball, volleyball and soccer, many weekend tournaments use Saturday for pool or preliminary play and Sunday for elimination rounds and championships.
  • That fuels cities' and towns' investments in sports complexes built to draw traveling families and their hotel and restaurant spending.

Zoom in: The average sports parent spends 3 hours, 23 minutes every day their child has a practice or game, including driving, attending activities, washing uniforms, preparing meals and communicating with coaches.

  • Families are spending heavily, too: The average sports family spent an average of $1,016 on a child's primary sport in 2024, up 46% from 2019, Aspen found.

What they're saying: Tim Morey, lead pastor at Life Covenant Church in Torrance, Calif., tells Axios that sports don't necessarily sever families from church, but they make attendance "more spotty" at times.

  • "If we inadvertently teach our kids that sports (are) more important than weekly worship, then everything is more important than weekly worship."

Yes, but: Religious institutions are attempting to adapt rather than surrender.

  • Morey said some families "divide and conquer," sending one parent to church and the other to the field.
  • Others have kids attend the first 10 minutes of service in their sports uniforms or stream services live from team hotels.

Between the lines: Youth sports can create the same sense of community that mirrors what church did — to a point, Flanagan said.

  • Parents form tight bonds because they spend so much time together, but competition for positions and playing time can also strain those relationships, Flanagan said.

The bottom line: For generations, Sunday was about getting the family closer to heaven.

  • For many families today, Sunday can also be about getting a daughter closer to UCLA's softball team.

item.title: Christa Pike left the hospital and returned to Tennessee prison after failed lethal injection
item.description:
Tennessee inmate Christa Pike was released from the hospital and is back in prison more than a week after she survived the state's attempt to execute her by lethal injection, her attorneys said Saturday.

The big picture: The failed execution was unprecedented. Pike, 50, got two doses of the deadly drug pentobarbital on Sept. 30 and was still breathing.

  • The state called an ambulance and Pike got life-saving care at a local hospital.
  • Pike's attorneys said they believed she was "brain dead" and on life support. It shocked them and her doctors when she woke up and began talking earlier this week.

What they're saying: Pike's attorneys said she had returned to Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she had been housed for decades.

  • "She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," the attorneys said in a statement.
  • "She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery."

Catch up quick: Gov. Bill Lee ordered an independent review to determine how Pike was able to survive the attempted lethal injection. Another execution set for December was called off while that investigation plays out.

Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.

item.title: JD Vance says he won't watch livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter
item.description:
Vice President JD Vance said Friday he won't watch a potential livestream of the convicted Fort Hood shooter's execution, which President Trump told reporters he had approved.

Why it matters: Vance questioned whether the execution would actually be public but joined a small chorus of Republicans opposed to watching the execution, which is set to be conducted by a firing squad in December.

What they're saying: "Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance told reporters on Friday.

  • "Now that said, I mean, look, if it's all through livestream, I'm not going to be watching it."

Yes, but: Trump's comments came during a separate press gaggle on Friday, where he was asked if he had authorized or approved the livestream of the execution.

  • "Did I approve? Absolutely, I approve."

Driving the news: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in an interview Thursday that Americans would be able to watch the execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting.

  • "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it. ... People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," he said.
  • AP later reported that the execution would be livestreamed.
  • If it goes forward, Hasan's execution will be the first public one in 90 years, and the first military execution since 1961.

Zoom in: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) condemned plans to make the execution public in a Thursday night X post.

  • "Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting. Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America," the outgoing senator said.
  • Utah Sen. John Curtis (R) said in an X post, "Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent."
  • "A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment. Secretary Hegseth's plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite. The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity."

The other side: Some GOP politicians, like Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.), welcomed the livestream.

  • "Excellent. Public execution is what this terrorist deserves. We will be watching," he said in a post on X.

Editor's note: This story was updated with comments from President Trump.

item.title: The surprising post-pandemic drop in income inequality
item.description:
Data: Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios

Middle- and lower-earners' inflation-adjusted incomes rose during the Biden years — but high earners saw their incomes fall.

  • That's a surprising finding from one of the most thorough datasets on American household finances, released Friday morning by the Federal Reserve.

Why it matters: The data sheds granular new information on a much-contested question: What happened to Americans' real incomes during the post-pandemic period? It featured an exceptionally tight job market and the highest inflation in decades, followed by aggressive Fed rate hikes.

  • The median American family's income rose 7% in inflation-adjusted terms between 2021 and 2024. But that masked significant differences among income brackets.
  • The average real income of families in the top 10% of earners fell 14%, to $652,000 from $757,000 (both figures are 2025 dollars).
  • That implies, contrary to a common narrative about the K-shaped economy, that income inequality fell during the post-pandemic period.

Yes, but: The story for wealth is very different. Families that were already wealthy — and tend to own stocks, houses and other assets — became much richer from 2022 to 2025.

  • Among families in the top 10% of income, median net worth rose a whopping 31% from 2022 to 2025, compared with a 2% rise in net worth for the median family.
  • Families in the bottom 40% of income actually saw their net worth decline slightly in that span.

The intrigue: The data, from the Survey of Consumer Finances, is collected and released every three years. Friday morning's release is the 2025 survey — but questions about income cover the preceding calendar year.

  • As such, the income numbers compare 2024 with 2021 — conveniently capturing the change from the early part of the Biden administration to near its end.

Between the lines: While the compression in income inequality seen in this data may seem surprising, it aligns with other evidence that blue-collar workers saw bigger raises during the super-tight job market and inflationary episode of 2021 and 2022 than did higher-earning white-collar professionals.

  • Moreover, in a footnote, the Fed researchers note that top earners tend to have income from volatile sources, mainly capital gains and business income.
  • Big swings in those income sources among the highest earners can create outsized movement in the averages.

Of note: The survey also sheds light on how the Fed's aggressive interest rate hikes in 2022 and 2023, meant to bring inflation under control, hammered borrowers.

  • The median debt payment-to-income ratio rose 2 percentage points from 2022 to 2025, reaching 15.4%.
  • The share of families with debt payment-to-income ratios above 40%, a threshold for high debt obligations, increased to 8.6% from 6.5%, reaching a level last seen in the 2013 survey.

The bottom line: Low earners saw bigger percentage gains in their incomes' purchasing power amid the post-pandemic inflation than did high earners — but the rich got a lot richer at the same time.

item.title: Navi Pillay, advocate for international law, wins Nobel Peace Prize
item.description:
Navi Pillay, an outspoken supporter of international law who has served as a judge on multiple global courts and as the UN's top human rights official, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday.

Why it matters: President Trump once again did not win the prize he has openly coveted.

  • Pillay, among other posts, previously served on the International Criminal Court — a body Trump sanctioned and last month called "rogue" and "evil."

What they're saying: "The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 goes to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order," the prize committee said in a social media post.

  • "This year's laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted."

Background: Besides the ICC and the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, Pillay also served as the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and as chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

  • Pillay, 85 and a native of South Africa, began practicing law in the late 1960s and served on her country's high court before her international appointments.

Zoom out: Pillay stands for many of the ideas and institutions Trump has condemned.

  • Besides sanctioning the ICC, he withdrew the U.S. from the UN Human Rights Council last year.
  • He's also made a target of South Africa and its Black government, promising asylum to white South African farmers.
  • The AP reported that Pillay, reacting to the news, said world leaders have a "legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war."

The big picture: The Nobel Peace Prize is Trump's white whale, an honor he talks about constantly and has frequently insisted he should have won.

  • Last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, gave Trump her prize medal earlier this year — though the Norwegian Nobel Institute made clear the prize itself could not actually be transferred.

The intrigue: As of mid-morning Friday, Trump hadn't reacted publicly to the news — but he did repost a Truth Social post condemning Pillay and praising his accomplishments as a better choice for the prize.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with Trump's reaction.

Navi Pillay, an outspoken supporter of international law who has served as a judge on multiple global courts and as the UN's top human rights official, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday.

Why it matters: President Trump once again did not win the prize he has openly coveted.

  • Pillay, among other posts, previously served on the International Criminal Court — a body Trump sanctioned and last month called "rogue" and "evil."

What they're saying: "The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 goes to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order," the prize committee said in a social media post.

  • "This year's laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted."

Background: Besides the ICC and the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, Pillay also served as the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and as chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

  • Pillay, 85 and a native of South Africa, began practicing law in the late 1960s and served on her country's high court before her international appointments.

Zoom out: Pillay stands for many of the ideas and institutions Trump has condemned.

  • Besides sanctioning the ICC, he withdrew the U.S. from the UN Human Rights Council last year.
  • He's also made a target of South Africa and its Black government, promising asylum to white South African farmers.
  • The AP reported that Pillay, reacting to the news, said world leaders have a "legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war."

The big picture: The Nobel Peace Prize is Trump's white whale, an honor he talks about constantly and has frequently insisted he should have won.

  • Last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, gave Trump her prize medal earlier this year — though the Norwegian Nobel Institute made clear the prize itself could not actually be transferred.

The intrigue: As of mid-morning Friday, Trump hadn't reacted publicly to the news — but he did repost a Truth Social post condemning Pillay and praising his accomplishments as a better choice for the prize.

item.title: AI vs. the rest of the economy
item.description:
Data: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips; Note: Data center construction includes construction costs, such as labor, materials, profits of contractors, architectural and engineering work and miscellaneous overhead, interest and taxes. Does not include servers, racks, chips or memory.

More and more, it seems as if there's the AI economy — and everything else.

Why it matters: The growing chasm between the breakneck growth of the AI world and the slower pace of the economy where most Americans work and live has huge implications, especially for the markets.

Zoom in: The most recent numbers on U.S. construction spending through August — shown above — paint the picture remarkably clearly.

Zoom out: The same divide is an important theme in the markets as well.

  • In corporate bonds, AI-related offerings accounted for more than half of net investment grade issuance for the year through the end of August, according to data from Apollo and Bloomberg.
Data: Apollo, Bloomberg; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips

And of course, excitement over all things related to AI has supercharged the market values of Nvidia, the hyperscalers and other AI-related tech stocks.

Stunning stat: The weighting of the S&P 500 technology sector in terms of market capitalization is now roughly 40%. That's higher than during the peak of the dot-com bubble.

  • But that actually underplays the impact of AI.
  • If you throw in the hyperscalers Meta and Amazon, which S&P doesn't include in the tech sector, the share of the AI-pilled part of the blue-chip index climbs closer to 50%.
Data: FactSet, Axios; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips

The bottom line: The growth gap between AI and everything else means the U.S. economy and the markets are increasingly yoked to AI — and all the risks that come with it.

item.title: Scoop: AI companies plot "day after" scenarios for public revolt
item.description:
Top executives at Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI companies are privately gaming out scenarios for a public and political revolt after a catastrophic AI event.

Why it matters: These officials anticipate a large-scale event, most likely a cyberattack, that shuts down access to financial services, internet connectivity, or even power and water.

  • The first example of significant real-world harm caused by unsafe AI would turn an already wary public further against the technology and its leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, as well as President Trump for his reluctance to regulate it.

Threat level: While scenario planning is common within many companies and national security settings — the Pentagon has been running war games for decades — the difference is that many top AI researchers and executives believe a major incident is inevitable.

  • "OpenAI conducts preparedness exercises where teams discuss and work through a range of potential scenarios," a company spokesperson said. "These scenarios are not treated as inevitable, but are meant to help us prepare for a variety of circumstances."
  • Anthropic declined to comment.

Zoom in: The blame game will start whether a rogue-agent swarm breaks containment from an internal testing environment or a bad actor finds unexpected ways to use available models.

  • A recent campaign targeting South Korean financial organizations — including reported breaches at two banks — shows the damage one person can do.
  • A hacker from China allegedly used AI tools from China-developed models, including DeepSeek, to steal data from tens of thousands of bank customers. The attacker used Claude Code to ask for help finding places to sell the stolen data, according to cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike.

Top AI planners assume Democrats, ascendant after the midterms, will move fast to shut down AI but will face significant challenges.

  • An aging Congress, out of touch with the AI revolution, could find itself out of its depth.
  • The global economy is now heavily intertwined with an AI infrastructure buildout. Slowing it down could hit an already fragile economy hard.
  • Too many open-weight models can already be freely downloaded and used to cause harm, a problem most cybersecurity pros see as solvable only by using AI to fight rogue AI.

Between the lines: The planning involves red-teaming for worst-case scenarios. It focuses mainly on racing to educate members of Congress.

  • Company executives know regulation has no chance of passing right now, but still want to shape the legislation and policies U.S. leaders will turn to after a first catastrophic event.

What we're watching: Many AI industry insiders told Axios they believe a major event will occur in the next six to 12 months.

  • Even with Democrats in control of the House and Senate, the companies see fractured politics as the norm, including within the Democratic Party.
  • Some of the most heavy-handed Democratic proposals include banning superintelligence or pausing advanced AI development.
  • Others have bipartisan support and even some industry buy-in, including a required kill switch on advanced AI. But experts have questioned the viability of trying to turn off all AI systems.

The bottom line: In a real crisis, Washington can set partisan differences aside. One Democratic aide pointed to cooperation during COVID and the 2008 financial crisis.

item.title: Exclusive: Anthropic's plan to protect critical infrastructure
item.description:
Anthropic is launching a new cybersecurity initiative designed to bring its most powerful AI models and engineers to companies protecting power grids, water utilities and other critical infrastructure, the company first shared with Axios.

Why it matters: Critical infrastructure operators are struggling to secure aging, complex systems as AI threatens to make cyberattacks faster and cheaper to execute.

Driving the news: Under its new Critical Infrastructure Defense Program, Anthropic will provide its frontier AI models, onsite engineers and threat research to companies already responsible for securing critical infrastructure systems.

  • Participating companies will use these resources to identify and fix vulnerabilities in their customers' systems.
  • The program's founding partners include Accenture, Booz Allen Hamilton, CrowdStrike, Deloitte, Dragos, Hitachi, Insane Cyber, Nozomi Networks, Palo Alto Networks, PwC and Rockwell Automation.
  • Anthropic said several partners are already using Claude to fix vulnerabilities and help customers do the same.

Zoom in: Anthropic is also launching a free AI-powered vulnerability scanning service for open-source software projects, called OSS Scanner.

  • Participating projects will receive periodic scans from Claude, along with automated reports detailing vulnerabilities, how they could be exploited and suggested fixes.
  • The reports won't undergo human review before being sent to software maintainers, meaning some findings could be inaccurate.

The big picture: Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI developers are looking for ways to put their most powerful models in the hands of cyber defenders as hackers gain access to similar capabilities.

  • Anthropic's new initiative builds on lessons from Project Glasswing, which gave vetted organizations access to its most capable AI models to identify security vulnerabilities.
  • The company said the project demonstrated how quickly AI can uncover vulnerabilities, but also how difficult it remains to verify and fix them.

Yes, but: It's unclear how participating companies will safely test and deploy fixes without disrupting utilities' operations, one of the biggest challenges in securing critical infrastructure.

  • Anthropic also didn't specify whether partners will receive free model access or who will cover the computing costs associated with using its AI tools.

Go deeper: AI is supercharging hacks of everyday utilities

item.title: Trump: Anyone saying "AI" is "THE ENEMY!" The White House uses it
item.description:
President Trump on Thursday called anyone who uses "Artificial Intelligence" instead of "Super Intelligence" "THE ENEMY!" — even as the White House continues using the term "AI."

Why it matters: Trump's push to rebrand AI as "super intelligence" clashes with established terminology in the technology industry.

  • Trump's branding blurs the distinction between AI and super intelligence, a hypothetical version of AI more advanced than human intelligence.

What they're saying: "The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday.

Zoom out: Trump's executive order from September doubled down on using "SI" over "AI," though it did not offer a penalty for using the term.

  • The order specifically defines "Super Intelligence" using the existing federal legal definition of AI.
  • The order calls on federal agencies to change how they describe AI in official communications.
  • The State Department already ordered diplomats to use the term after Trump's United Nations speech on Sept. 22.

Yes, but: The White House still uses "AI" as a term, including on the Office of Science and Technology Policy website, which makes reference to "artificial intelligence."

  • On Thursday, the White House updated its AI.gov website to read "SI.gov" in a massive font. The URL is still "AI.gov," though, with "SI.gov" leading to an error page.
  • When an Axios reporter asked the America.gov chatbot about AI, the bot responded: "The executive branch uses Super Intelligence (SI) for this topic, not the older term you used."

What we're watching: Whether the White House could update its websites to reflect Trump's preferred terminology.

  • The White House did not respond to Axios' request for comment Thursday.

Editor's note: This article has been updated to reflect the White House's change of its AI.gov website to read "SI.gov."

item.title: Labor Department marks low layoffs milestone
item.description:
Data: U.S. Department of Labor; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

New applications for unemployment benefits have stayed below 200,000 in a stretch rarely seen in modern history.

  • Jobless claims fell by 2,000, to 197,000, last week, the Labor Department said Thursday morning.

Why it matters: It points to a remarkable stability on the "firing" side of the labor market, even amid a slower pace of hiring on the other side of the equation.

  • That is helping to keep unemployment low, but it also masks a growing divide between Americans who have jobs and those struggling to find one.

What they're saying: "New jobless claims have been under 200,000 for a month now, an incredibly low level of layoffs for a sustained period of time that hasn't been seen since the 1960s," Navy Federal Credit Union chief economist Heather Long said.

By the numbers: The four-week average, which smooths out weekly volatility, fell to 198,000, its lowest level since the red-hot job market of 2022–2023.

The other side: Jobless claims don't capture every layoff. Some workers receive severance, don't qualify for benefits or find the application process too cumbersome.

  • Still, when layoffs have surged across the economy, claims have surged with them — including during the recessions after the financial crisis and the pandemic. The absence of such an increase now is hard to dismiss.
  • Other data tells a similar story: Announced job cuts fell 20% from a year earlier in September, according to outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

The bottom line: Employers may be reluctant to hire, but they appear just as reluctant to fire — an unusual combination that, for now, keeps the labor market on steady footing.

item.title: The Fed's going to take its time with rate hikes
item.description:
A couple more interest rate hikes are probably on the way. But the Federal Reserve is in no great hurry to deliver them. That's the takeaway from the latest round of communications out of the central bank.

Why it matters: It implies that the Fed is not in a full-scale effort to tighten the screws on the economy, but rather a cautious recalibration in light of inflationary pressures and robust growth.

  • With Fed chairman Kevin Warsh declining to offer much in the way of guidance, traders and Fed watchers must look to other communications for clues — and the message has been strikingly consistent across the latest crumbs of information.

Driving the news: Speaking Thursday morning in Istanbul, Fed governor Christopher Waller explained, with distinctly non-Warshian detail, what kind of interest rate path he anticipates.

  • "If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2 percent goal," he said.
  • "But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur. The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
  • That aligns with the language in the minutes of the September policy meeting released Wednesday afternoon, stating that "most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year-end," but that they "approached each meeting with an open mind."

Of note: The minutes and Waller comments come after fairly explicit comments last week from vice chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed president John Williams waving away expectations of a second rate increase at a meeting concluding Oct. 28.

Zoom in: That doesn't answer the question of how big this tightening cycle will turn out to be. But the tea leaves point to one more rate hike at this year's final meeting and another early in 2027.

  • That would amount to a total of 0.75 percentage point of rate increases, the same size adjustment as easing cycles in 2019 and 2025.
  • Waller, in an extended musing about Fed communication strategy in Thursday morning's speech, used a 0.75-point adjustment as the hypothetical cumulative adjustment. If nothing else, it's a hint that he sees three rate hikes in this adjustment cycle as the most probable course of action.

Between the lines: Warsh is determined to maintain optionality and not pre-commit to a policy path, and he still has that. But talk of leaving rates steady in October and keeping the cumulative adjustment modest tells us something about what kind of rate cycle Fed leadership envisions.

  • This is not — in their view, at least — the beginning of a sustained, open-ended tightening cycle needed to slow the economy and break the back of inflation, as last seen in 2022.
  • Rather, it's a take-your-time, limited operation to better calibrate policy for the mix of solid labor market results, accelerating growth and elevated inflation that they see.

What they're saying: "With evidence that economic activity is strengthening in the second half of this year, I am not greatly concerned that tighter monetary policy threatens a damaging slowdown in the economy," Waller said Thursday morning.

  • "But I am concerned that the recent acceleration in inflation — after what soon will be five and a half years of it above the FOMC's target — will lead consumers, investors, and price-setting businesses to revise up their expectations for future inflation."

The bottom line: Investors can take solace that the Fed is not preparing aggressive action to take away the punchbowl. The open question is whether this limited tightening will do the trick in getting inflation down faster.

item.title: "The Axios Show": Inside Bryan Johnson's quest to make 300 the new 70
item.description:
Bryan Johnson, the face of the longevity movement, wants to make staying alive more important than making money.

  • The famous/infamous biohacker spends over $2 million a year on his health, talks about living forever and publicly tracks everything from his erections to his sperm strength.

Why it matters: As Johnson fights to "live forever," he's doing so with a wink to his 8 million social media followers, a link to his business in his bio and a knack for drawing attention to himself.

What they're saying: In his interview with The Axios Show, he offered some advice for Elon Musk, said he'd love to help President Trump with his health and revealed his ultimate goal.

  • "Will the 25th century ... be like, 'thank you' in 500 years? Will they give me a head nod? That's the goal," he said.

Zoom out: His big picture focus: change the focus of society to health, not wealth.

  • "Society says making money... is the greatest trophy one can get...we are at this inflection moment as a species where we are transitioning to 'Don't Die,'" Johnson said, referring to the title of his longevity movement.
  • "What creates status and power and prestige is going to be different. And as crazy as it sounds, it may be your nighttime erections...It may be your ability to dunk a basketball at age 49," he said.
  • Johnson, 49, is currently trying to dunk.

Zoom out: That focus is what drives some of his more extreme experiments and interventions.

  • In 2023, Johnson injected his teenage son's plasma, which he found to be a helpful regimen for his dad but not for himself, saying his own biomarkers are already "pretty similar to my 18-year-old."
  • Through the help of wearables, tests and a concierge team, Johnson has gathered over 4.2 billion data points about his own body and health, and he relies on AI tools to help parse takeaways from that data.
  • He has an in-home medical lab of sorts where he can do continuous testing, monitoring and procedures.

Zoom in: Perhaps his most extreme act is his online presence, which Johnson called "performance art" in our conversation.

  • When talking about humans dramatically increasing lifespans through scientific methods, "no one cares," he said. But "if you talk about it in performance art where it has a vibe and an energy to it, people will engage."

The intrigue: Still, even Johnson recommends many of the basics for health: sleep, healthy diet and exercise.

  • For those who want to go further, he recommends a blood draw or MRI, sitting in a sauna several times a week and testing out psychedelics.
  • When asked which longevity treatments feel like snake oil, Johnson said "Basically everything on social media."
